transcript:
Meeting Header
Date/Time: 2026-03-19 16:00 PST
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Ava Martinez (Redwood AE), Lucas Kim (Redwood SE), Priya Das (Silverline CTO), Mark Reynolds (Sr. ML Engineer), Erin Cole (Procurement)
Link to deck: short.redwood/demo-streaming

Summary: quick hosted API walkthrough focused on chat and text gen basics — streaming, params (temperature/top_p/max_tokens), and retries/idempotency. Customer is evaluating hosted vs dedicated for a customer-facing chat assistant; primary concerns: latency, cost, and data residency / compliance.

Topics Covered: hosted API overview; streaming mechanics; parameter tuning; retry/backoff and idempotency patterns; console demo of request logs and token breakdown; Optimize suggestions (batching, caching) briefly; security/compliance notes.

Transcript Body:
[00:00] Ava Martinez: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Ava from Redwood, AE on the West. We also have Lucas, our SE. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Priya Das: Good thanks, Priya here. We kicked off just a bit late, sorry. Excited to see the streaming stuff.
[00:10] Lucas Kim: Hi Priya, Mark, Erin — Lucas here. I'll jump into the demo after a quick overview.
[00:18] Ava Martinez: Quick agenda: 1) high-level hosted API features, 2) live console/demo streaming, 3) params and tuning, 4) retries and idempotency patterns, 5) recap & next steps. Anything to add?
[00:26] Mark Reynolds: No that's fine. We mostly want to understand performance tradeoffs and how to integrate streaming into our webchat.
[00:30] Ava Martinez: Great.
[00:33] Lucas Kim: Alright, quick high-level. Redwood's hosted API supports chat and text generation, streaming via SSE or websockets, and first-class SDKs. For streaming we send incremental deltas, so your UI can render tokens as they arrive — reduces perceived latency. Typical latencies for our curated models are 80-300ms per token on gpu-backed endpoints depending on model size and region.
[00:48] Priya Das: 80 to 300ms per token, is that median? And what's the average end-to-end for a 100-token response?
[00:55] Lucas Kim: Good q. 80-300ms is single-token latency distribution; end-to-end for 100 tokens tends to be around 2-8s depending on batching, KV cache hits, and model. If you're doing prefix caching for common prompts you often see much lower.
[01:12] Mark Reynolds: You said KV cache — is that the same as the key-value cache for transformer past-key values?
[01:15] Lucas Kim: Yeah, although sometimes our transcription's messy — it's K V cache, yes. It stores past KV so repeated continuations are faster.
[01:21] Priya Das: Can you demo streaming integration? We have a React chat and want to know whether to use SSE or websockets.
[01:27] Lucas Kim: For browser apps SSE works well and is simpler — chunked transfer of tokens. Websockets gives bi-directional control if you need midstream cancellation or interactive tools. I'll show a small example in the console.
[01:36] [Demo starts — Lucas shares screen]
[01:40] Lucas Kim: Here's the console. I fire a chat.create request. If you look at the network trace you can see the chunked SSE frames, each with a "delta" token. In our JS SDK it's one line — client.chat.stream — and you get token events.
[01:54] Priya Das: That looks good. How do retries work when streaming? If the connection drops midstream, do we replay?
[02:00] Lucas Kim: Good point. For streamed responses we recommend using idempotency keys at the request-level. On disconnect, you can either resume if you stored the streaming offset client-side (we have a resume token pattern for dedicated customers), or you can re-request with the idempotency key and Redwood will return the stored final result if the prior attempt completed server-side. For partials, best practice is to detect incomplete finalization and re-run the request with the same key.
[02:21] Mark Reynolds: Is there server-side storage for streaming state on hosted? Any extra cost?
[02:25] Lucas Kim: We persist minimal metadata for idempotency and final outputs for a short TTL — default 24 hours for hosted. No extra charge for idempotency metadata, standard token billing applies for compute.
[02:35] Priya Das: How about retry/backoff patterns in the SDKs?
[02:38] Lucas Kim: SDKs implement exponential backoff with jitter by default and respect 429s and 503s. For critical requests we recommend up to 3 retries with backoff starting at 500ms, doubling. Also use idempotency keys to avoid duplicate side effects.
[02:51] [00:03 silence as demo loads, some typing noises]
[03:05] Ava Martinez: Quick note on params: temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop sequences. Lower temperature and top_p narrows outputs and reduces variance — useful for deterministic flows like retrieval-augmented generation. Max_tokens controls the size/billing of the response. For cost/latency tune max_tokens and prefer prefix caching and batching.
[03:23] Priya Das: We have a use case where the assistant should be short. Any guardrails to enforce max length server-side?
[03:28] Lucas Kim: Yes, you can configure hard max tokens on a per-route basis in the console — prevents runaway outputs. Also we support response filters and structured output to ensure you get JSON back.
[03:35] Mark Reynolds: About batching: we have many low-latency queries per second. Would batching hurt our latency?
[03:40] Lucas Kim: There's a tradeoff. Continuous batching groups requests for GPU efficiency; you can set SLOs in routing policy. For tight latency SLOs, you can set low batch windows and risk higher cost. Our Optimize tool suggests batch size settings after analysing your traffic patterns.
[03:52] Priya Das: Any numbers on cost differences between streaming small replies vs single big blocking call?
[03:56] Lucas Kim: Streaming doesn't change token billing; it's still per-token. But streaming can reduce perceived latency and allow aggressive client-side cancellation which can reduce total tokens consumed in some flows. Cost differences are mostly about model size and caching hits.
[04:10] Erin Cole: From procurement side — what compliance docs do you provide? SOC2, ISO, encryption?
[04:14] Ava Martinez: We provide SOC 2 Type II report, ISO documents on request, and integrations with customer KMS for Private deployments. Hosted has encrypted-at-rest keys managed by us, with options for Bring-Your-Own-Key on Dedicated/Private. I'll attach the security pack.
[04:29] Priya Das: Data residency — we need EU-only processing for some customers. Does hosted support region pinning?
[04:33] Lucas Kim: Yes, we have region selection for hosted endpoints and VPC/private options for stronger isolation. For strict residency we often recommend Private deployment. But region pinning in hosted works for many customers.
[04:45] Mark Reynolds: Can you show the logs / token breakdown?
[04:49] [Lucas navigates to per-request trace]
[04:51] Lucas Kim: Here is the per-request breakdown — token count, cost estimate, latency per stage (scheduling, queueing, inference). You can hook these into our tracing hooks. Also we expose route-level rollouts so you can canary a model.
[05:05] Priya Das: If we hit errors mid-call, do you surface structured error codes?
[05:09] Lucas Kim: Yes 4xx/5xx with structured JSON: code, retriable boolean, message. SDK surfaces them as exceptions with metadata like request_id and suggested retry.
[05:18] Ava Martinez: Quick question — are you leaning hosted or dedicated for the pilot?
[05:22] Priya Das: We're leaning hosted for speed but want to evaluate SLAs and whether we can get BYOK later. Also procurement will likely ask about long-term reserved pricing if we scale.
[05:31] Ava Martinez: Understandable. We support a transition path from hosted -> dedicated with identical API and rollouts. Pricing for reserved capacity is in the pricing sheet I'll send.
[05:40] Mark Reynolds: One more technical: how do you handle function-calling or tool calls in streaming mode?
[05:45] Lucas Kim: We stream deltas for function calls too — you get the structured JSON incrementally. We also ensure atomic function result delivery in the SDK. If you need guaranteed full JSON then use the non-streaming finalization endpoint, or have the SDK buffer the stream until the complete structure is received.
[05:59] Priya Das: Any gotchas when integrating with our existing auth? We use SAML SSO for internal tools and a proxy for webchat.
[06:06] Ava Martinez: For the console and team access we support SSO/SAML, SCIM for provisioning, and RBAC. API keys for the app are separate; you can store them behind your proxy or use short-lived tokens from our auth exchange.
[06:17] [Small cross-talk]
[06:22] Lucas Kim: Final part: retries and idempotency patterns I showed earlier — here's a quick cURL example in the console using --header "Idempotency-Key: <uuid>". For streaming client retry, detect partial stream + status != 200 and re-issue. For high scale, implement client dedupe by request hash.
[06:36] Priya Das: That helps. Could you share the SDK example and a checklist for production hardening?
[06:40] Ava Martinez: Yes, Lucas will share an example repo. We'll also include a prod checklist: token rotation, rate limiting, monitoring token usage, configuring max_tokens, and using idempotency.
[06:49] Mark Reynolds: Ok, timeline — we want to pilot a single region hosted integration in 2 weeks and run a 2-week load test. Is that realistic?
[06:55] Lucas Kim: Yes, we can support that. We'll help with baseline traffic patterns and sample load scripts.
[06:59] Erin Cole: Procurement asked for contract and reserved pricing example — will you send that?
[07:03] Ava Martinez: I'll send hosted pricing and reserved pricing examples.
[07:07] [Wrap-up]
[07:09] Ava Martinez: Recap: we'll send pricing + security pack, Lucas will share streaming SDK examples and retry patterns, Priya will confirm pilot scope and compliance needs. Schedule follow-up POC scoping for week of 3/30.
[07:19] Priya Das: Sounds good, thanks everyone.
[07:21] Mark Reynolds: Thanks.
[07:23] Erin Cole: Thanks.

Notes on transcription: occasional noise, speaker overlap at 06:17, some product terms transcribed inconsistently (K V cache vs KV cache).

References/Links Mentioned: short.redwood/demo-streaming, short.redwood/security-pack, repo.redwood/streaming-examples
